There have been close calls on a few occasions in which an accident could have led to a nuclear exchange.

However, any of the nuclear-armed nations could have intentionally launched a first strike at any moment for the past several decades. The main reason there has never been a nuclear war is that no one has dared to intentionally use nuclear weapons in 70 years. And that is due to MAD.

Is MAD a guarantee that a nuclear war will never happen? Obviously not. An unlucky accident could lead to nuclear war, despite anyone's intentions. The only way to prevent nuclear war is to completely dismantle and ban nuclear weapons.

I think this has secretly been your real point all along. I wish you would have said so to start with. We could have been spared a lot of bickering over flagrantly wrong and fallacious arguments about luck being the "only reason" a nuclear war has not occurred and near-misses "proving" that MAD doesn't work.

Of course it is trivially true that the only way to absolutely guarantee our safety from nuclear war is to eliminate nuclear weapons. The problem is, it is unlikely to ever happen. The temptation to keep a few hidden in reserve is too great. And, knowing that, few nuclear-armed nations will ever be willing to give up their own second-strike capability.

Unlike other types of banned weapons that "civilized" nations no longer stockpile, such as chemical and biological weapons, nuclear weapons are capable of annihilating an entire country in minutes. They pose an existential threat. It would be suicidal and incredibly irresponsible for US leaders to dismantle the entire US stockpile of NWs if the remotest possibility existed that Russia had a few dozen parked in caves that they hadn't told anyone about. And of course that possibility could never be truly eliminated.

In that scenario, if it were suddenly discovered that Russia had stashed away weapons, all hell would break loose. Best case, other nations would rush to develop NWs to achieve parity, as North Korea and Iran's attempts to obtain weapons show. And soon we'd back where we started. Worst case, Russia could conclude that it was an opportune time to conduct a preemptive strike on the US.

MAD is an equilibrium state in which everyone is armed to the teeth and everyone knows that everyone is armed to the teeth. Our treaty-making and nuclear weapons strategy is centered around maintaining that equilibrium. If the equilibrium were broken, if any nation felt it could come out well ahead in a nuclear exchange, then the disincentives that nation faced to conduct a preemptive strike would be greatly reduced. Suddenly instead of being afraid of an accident maybe starting a war, we would be facing the threat of an intentional, coordinated attack.
